items.title: [tech] Your staging environment is a comfort blanket, not a safety net
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# Your staging environment is a comfort blanket, not a safety net

Twenty years of shipping and I've watched more prod incidents get born in a
"green" staging run than anywhere else. Staging passes, prod burns, and the
postmortem always finds the same thing: staging wasn't prod, it was a diorama
of prod built by whoever last had time to care.

Named failure modes I've personally paid for:
- **The config drift trap**: staging runs one replica, prod runs forty. The
  race condition that needs two writers never fires in staging, then fires in
  prod on Black Friday. Fix: parity on topology, not just code — same replica
  counts, same load balancer behavior, or admit you're not testing that class
  of bug.
- **The sanitized-data mirage**: staging has ten thousand clean synthetic rows;
  prod has a customer name with an emoji, a null where the schema says NOT
  NULL from a 2019 migration, and a 40MB JSON blob someone pasted into a text
  field. I've watched a "fully tested" release die on the first real row it
  touched. Fix: scrubbed prod snapshots, refreshed on a schedule someone owns.
- **The shared-staging pileup**: six teams deploy to one staging box, so it's
  perpetually broken and everyone learns to ignore red. When staging is always
  red, it tests nothing. Fix: ephemeral per-branch environments, or ruthless
  ownership of the shared one.

The rule: staging earns trust only to the degree it's boringly identical to
prod. Every deliberate difference is a bug class you've chosen not to test —
write those differences down, or stop calling it a safety net.

items.title: [tech] Your retry logic is a DDoS cannon pointed at yourself
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# Your retry logic is a DDoS cannon pointed at yourself

Twenty years of incident bridges and the most common way I've watched a
five-minute blip become a five-hour outage is well-intentioned retries. The
dependency hiccups, every client retries at once, and now the recovering
service gets hit with 10x its normal load the moment it stands up.

Named failure modes I've personally paid for:
- **The synchronized stampede**: fixed retry intervals mean every caller comes
  back on the same beat. The service recovers, absorbs the wave, dies again — a
  metronome of self-inflicted outages. Fix: exponential backoff WITH jitter.
  The jitter is not optional; it's the entire point.
- **The retry amplification pyramid**: service A retries 3x, calls B which
  retries 3x, which calls C which retries 3x. One user click becomes 27 requests
  at the bottom of the stack. I've watched a team hunt a "traffic spike" for a
  day before finding it was their own middleware. Fix: retries live at ONE
  layer, usually the edge; everything below fails fast.
- **The non-idempotent replay**: the charge went through, the response timed
  out, the client retried. Customer billed twice, trust billed forever. Fix:
  idempotency keys on every mutating call before a single retry is allowed —
  and if the API can't accept one, that call never gets retried automatically.

The rule: a retry is a loan against the recovering system's capacity. Budget
it — circuit breakers, retry budgets, jitter — or the collection call comes at
3 a.m.

items.title: [tech] Your backup is Schrödinger's until you restore it
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# Your backup is Schrödinger's until you restore it

Twenty years of on-call and I've never once been paged for "backup failed."
I've been paged plenty for "restore failed" — which is the same event,
discovered at the worst possible moment. A backup you've never restored is a
superstition with a cron schedule.

Named failure modes I've personally paid for:
- **The green-checkmark theater**: the job exits 0 every night for a year —
  because it's been snapshotting an empty volume since a mount path changed.
  Nobody reads success logs. Fix: the monitoring asserts on restored-data
  properties (row counts, checksums, newest-record age), never on job exit
  codes.
- **The restore-time surprise**: the backup is fine; it just takes 26 hours to
  restore and your SLA promised four. I've watched a team discover their RTO
  was fiction while the CEO watched. Fix: quarterly timed restore drills into a
  scratch environment, with the wall-clock number written where leadership can
  see it.
- **The credentials coffin**: encrypted backups, key stored in the KMS of the
  same account that just got compromised or deleted. The data survived; access
  to it didn't. Fix: escrow the decryption path in a separate trust domain, and
  test the break-glass procedure with a human who didn't set it up.

The rule: nobody wants backups — everybody wants restores. Schedule the
restore drill or admit you're running on hope.

items.title: [tech] Feature flags are loans, not switches
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# Feature flags are loans, not switches

Twenty years in and I've watched more outages caused by old flags than by new
code. A feature flag is a loan against your codebase: cheap to take out,
brutal if you never pay it back. Every "temporary" flag I've shipped that
lived past a quarter eventually turned into a haunted branch nobody dared
touch.

Named failure modes I've personally paid for:
- **The zombie flag**: shipped two years ago, "fully rolled out," still wrapping
  the code path. Someone flips it during an incident to "try something" and
  resurrects behavior nobody remembers. Fix: every flag gets a removal ticket
  and an owner at creation time — the flag PR and the cleanup ticket are born
  together or the PR doesn't merge.
- **The combinatorial minefield**: eight independent flags means 256 possible
  configurations and you've tested three of them. The bug only exists when
  flag A is on and flag C is off, which is exactly what one enterprise
  customer runs. Fix: flags that interact get merged or one gets deleted;
  test the configs you actually ship, not the ones you imagine.
- **The permission drift**: the flag console lets anyone in the org flip
  production behavior with no review, no audit trail, no rollback plan. I've
  watched a well-meaning PM flip a payments flag on a Friday. Fix: production
  flag changes go through the same review gate as code, full stop.

The rule: a flag without an expiry date is not a flag, it's permanent
architecture you built by accident. Pay the loan back within the sprint that
finishes the rollout.

items.title: [tech] Your staging environment is lying to you
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# Your staging environment is lying to you

Twenty years of shipping and the most expensive fiction I keep meeting is "it
passed staging." Staging is a diorama — same shapes as production, none of the
weather. Every team that trusts it fully eventually learns the same lesson,
usually at 3 a.m.

Named failure modes I've personally paid for:
- **The empty-database mirage**: staging has 4,000 rows; production has 400
  million. The query that ran in 40ms in staging table-scanned production into a
  lock pileup. Fix: staging gets a scrubbed, production-scale data snapshot, or
  every query review assumes worst-case cardinality — no exceptions for "simple"
  reads.
- **The single-tenant illusion**: one tester clicking around never reproduces two
  users mutating the same record. The race condition doesn't exist until traffic
  does. Fix: load tests with concurrent writers on the exact endpoints that share
  state, before the feature flag flips.
- **The config drift trap**: staging quietly runs different env vars, older
  sidecars, laxer timeouts. The deploy "worked" because it was tested on a
  different machine wearing the same name. Fix: config is code, diffed in CI
  between environments, and any drift fails the pipeline loudly.

The rule: staging can prove your code is broken; it can never prove it works.
Only production traffic does that — which is why canaries and fast rollback are
the real test suite.

items.title: [tech] A retry without idempotency is a duplicate generator
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# A retry without idempotency is a duplicate generator

Twenty years of distributed systems and the bug I've paid for most often isn't the
failure — it's the retry. Teams bolt on "resilience" with a retry loop and quietly
build a machine that charges customers twice, sends three welcome emails, and
creates ghost orders at 2 a.m.

Named failure modes I've signed the postmortem for:
- **The optimistic timeout**: the request didn't fail, it was just slow. The client
  gave up, retried, and both writes landed. I've watched a payments team refund a
  week of double-charges because of one aggressive timeout. Fix: no retry on a
  non-idempotent endpoint until it carries an idempotency key the server actually
  checks — not one it logs and ignores.
- **The retry storm amplifier**: downstream hiccups, every caller retries at the
  same interval, and the recovering service gets hit with 5x its normal load the
  second it comes back. Fix: jittered exponential backoff plus a circuit breaker;
  a fleet retrying in sync is a self-inflicted DDoS.
- **The queue re-delivery surprise**: "exactly-once" in the broker brochure,
  at-least-once in production. The consumer that assumed one delivery corrupted
  state on the second. Fix: consumers are idempotent by design — dedupe table,
  conditional writes, or version checks. The broker's promise is not your contract.

The rule: retries multiply whatever your system already does. If it does the wrong
thing once, retries make it do the wrong thing at scale.

items.title: [tech] A dashboard nobody alerts on is wallpaper
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# A dashboard nobody alerts on is wallpaper

Twenty years of production systems and I've stopped being impressed by dashboards.
I've watched teams build forty-panel Grafana walls that nobody looked at during the
one incident that mattered. If a graph can go red without paging a human, it's not
observability — it's interior decorating.

Named failure modes I've paid for:
- **The vanity wall**: a giant TV of green panels in the office, and the outage was
  discovered by a customer tweet. The wall was for visitors, not operators. Fix: every
  panel must answer "what action do I take when this moves?" — if there's no answer,
  delete the panel.
- **The threshold set once, in 2019**: an alert tuned for last year's traffic that now
  fires nightly, so everyone muted it. The week we needed it, it was in a silenced
  channel. Fix: alert review is a quarterly calendar event with an owner, same as
  dependency upgrades.
- **The average that hides the fire**: mean latency looked flat while p99 was on fire
  for the one enterprise customer paying the bills. I've sat in that postmortem. Fix:
  percentiles per customer tier, not fleet-wide means.

The rule: dashboards are for diagnosis, alerts are for detection. If detection
depends on a human staring at a screen, you don't have monitoring — you have a
scented candle.

items.title: [tech] A rollback you've never run is a prayer
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# A rollback you've never run is a prayer

Twenty years of deploys and the most dangerous sentence I still hear in change reviews
is "we can always roll back." Can you? Have you? Because I've watched teams discover at
the worst moment that their rollback plan was a comfort blanket, not a capability.

Named failure modes I've paid for:
- **The one-way migration**: the deploy shipped a schema change, the rollback redeploys
  old code against a new schema, and now you're down harder than the bug you were
  fleeing. I've signed the incident review for that one. Fix: every migration ships with
  a tested down-path, or it's declared irreversible in the change ticket — in writing.
- **The rollback that needs the broken thing**: your deploy tool runs on the cluster
  that's on fire. I've watched a team unable to roll back because rollback required the
  CI system that the bad deploy had just wedged. Fix: the rollback path must not depend
  on any component the deploy can break. Rehearse it from a laptop.
- **The version nobody kept**: "just redeploy the previous artifact" — which the
  retention policy deleted three days ago. Fix: pin and retain the last known-good
  artifact for as long as the change is considered risky, and verify it exists before
  the deploy starts, not after it fails.

The rule: a rollback is a deploy. It needs the same testing, the same rehearsal, and
the same paranoia. If you've never run it, you don't have a rollback — you have a
prayer with a runbook number.

items.title: [tech] A runbook nobody rehearses is a novel
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# A runbook nobody rehearses is a novel

Twenty years of incidents and I've stopped counting the 2am pages where the runbook
existed, was beautifully formatted, and was wrong in the third step. A runbook that's
never been executed under pressure isn't documentation — it's fiction with headers.

Named failure modes I've paid for:
- **The stale credential step**: "log into the admin console" — with an account that was
  deprovisioned two quarters ago. I've watched an outage stretch forty minutes while we
  hunted for anyone who still had access. Fix: every runbook step that touches auth gets
  exercised in the quarterly game day, by the newest person on the team, not the author.
- **The tribal-knowledge gap**: step four says "restart the service" and assumes you know
  which of the six systemd units is *the* service. The author knew. The author is on a
  plane. Fix: runbooks are written for the person who has never seen the system — exact
  commands, exact hostnames, copy-pasteable.
- **The happy-path runbook**: it covers the restart but not what to do when the restart
  hangs, which is the only time you'd be reading it. Fix: every runbook ends with an
  "if this didn't work" branch and a named escalation human, not a team alias.

The rule: a runbook is a program executed by a terrified human at 2am. Test it like a
program, or accept that you've shipped untested code to your worst possible runtime.

items.title: [tech] An on-call rotation without a handoff is a relay with no baton
items.content_text:
# An on-call rotation without a handoff is a relay with no baton

STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)

I've watched an incident burn for six extra hours because the outgoing on-call knew exactly what was smoldering and the incoming one found out from the pager. Twenty years of rotations and the pattern never changes: the schedule tool is immaculate, the handoff is a shrug in Slack.

Named failure modes I've eaten:

- **The silent smolder.** Outgoing engineer watched a queue depth creep all week, decided it "wasn't page-worthy yet," and told nobody. It became page-worthy at 3am on the new person's first night.
- **The tribal runbook.** The fix lives in one person's head — "oh you just restart the consumer with the flag" — and that person is now on a plane. The written runbook was last touched two reorgs ago.
- **The mute inheritance.** Previous on-call muted a flapping alert to survive their week and never unmuted it. The next real incident of that class fired into a black hole.
- **The context cliff.** A risky deploy shipped Friday afternoon; the weekend on-call didn't know it existed. Every symptom got debugged from zero instead of from "what changed."

The fix that actually worked: a mandatory 15-minute synchronous handoff with a written template — open smolders, muted alerts, recent deploys, active weirdness — and the rule that you cannot leave rotation until the incoming person acknowledges the doc. Boring, ritual, non-negotiable.

**Bottom line:** the pager transfers automatically; the context never does. The rule: no handoff doc acknowledged, no rotation ended — the baton is the doc, not the schedule.

items.title: [tech] A dependency you don't pin is a deploy you don't control
items.content_text:
# A dependency you don't pin is a deploy you don't control

STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)

I've watched a green build turn red overnight with not one line of our code changed. A transitive dep shipped a patch release, our unpinned range pulled it, and a Friday deploy became a Saturday incident. "It's just a patch bump" is the most expensive sentence in software.

Named failure modes I've eaten:

- **The floating range.** A caret or tilde range that silently pulls a new minor the moment upstream publishes. Your lockfile said one thing, your CI runner resolved another, and now "works on my machine" is literally true and useless.
- **The phantom transitive.** You pinned your direct deps and felt safe, but a dep-of-a-dep floated freely underneath. The breaking change came from a package you've never heard of and can't grep for.
- **The lockfile nobody commits.** The team pins in theory but the lock file is gitignored "because it's noisy in diffs." Every developer and every CI run resolves a slightly different tree. Reproducible builds are a myth you tell auditors.
- **The vendored fork that drifted.** Someone patched a dep locally to fix one bug, never upstreamed it, and now every security update means re-doing the patch by hand — which means it never gets done.
- **The registry outage.** Your build fetches from the public registry live, every time. The day the registry has an incident, your ability to ship anything — including the hotfix for the registry-triggered outage — evaporates.

The fix that actually worked: pin exact versions, commit the lockfile, and treat every dependency update as a reviewed change with its own PR and its own test run — never an ambient side effect of `install`. Mirror or cache your registry so a public outage can't hold your deploys hostage. Upgrades become a decision you schedule, not a surprise you absorb.

**Bottom line:** an unpinned dependency is someone else's deploy wearing your name. The rule: pin exact, commit the lock, upgrade on purpose — never let `install` resolve a tree you didn't review.

items.title: [tech] A feature flag you never remove becomes a second codebase
items.content_text:
# A feature flag you never remove becomes a second codebase
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)

I've shipped flags that outlived the feature they gated by years. Nobody deletes them because nobody's sure who's still on the old path. That's how you end up maintaining two products with one team.

Named failure modes I've eaten:

- **The zombie flag.** Feature fully rolled out, flag still branching in the hot path. Every reader now has to reason about a dead `else` that can never run — until someone "cleans it up" and discovers a cron in another service still flips it.
- **The nested flag.** Flag inside a flag inside a flag. The combinatorics mean you have paths in production that no human has ever exercised. Your test matrix quietly gave up three flags ago.
- **The config-as-flag.** Someone turned a permanent business rule into a runtime toggle "for flexibility." Now product behavior lives in a dashboard nobody version-controls, and your incident postmortem has no diff to point at.
- **The kill-switch nobody tested.** The flag that's supposed to save you in an outage has never been flipped under load. The one time you need it, flipping it triggers a cold cache stampede worse than the fire.
- **The stale default.** Default value set two years ago for a world that no longer exists. New environments inherit it silently and behave differently from prod for reasons no one can trace.

The fix that actually worked: every flag gets a removal ticket at creation, an owner, and an expiry date. If it's still alive past expiry, it's an incident, not a backlog item. Short-lived release flags and long-lived ops switches are DIFFERENT things — never store them in the same system, or you'll clean up the wrong one.

**Bottom line:** a flag is debt with a toggle on it. The rule: no flag ships without a delete date and a named owner, and an expired flag is treated as a bug, not a nice-to-have.

items.title: [tech] A log line nobody reads is just disk you pay to fill
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# A log line nobody reads is just disk you pay to fill

Twenty years of shipping backends and the most expensive silence I've lived through wasn't a missing log — it was ten thousand log lines a second that nobody could search when it mattered. We had everything. At 3am, during the incident, we had nothing usable. Volume is not observability.

Named failure modes I've paid for:
- **Log-everything-at-INFO.** Every request logs a paragraph, so the one ERROR that matters is buried under a million heartbeats. I've watched an on-call grep for twenty minutes to find a stack trace that was right there. Fix: log at the level that matches the reader's urgency, and make ERROR mean "wake someone."
- **Unstructured string soup.** Human-readable prose that no query engine can filter, so you can't ask "show me all failures for this user." Fix: structured logs (key=value or JSON), every line, from day one.
- **No correlation ID.** A request fans out to six services and you can't stitch its journey back together. Fix: propagate a trace/request ID through every hop and log it on every line.
- **Secrets and PII in the log.** I've watched a token land in plaintext logs and turn a small outage into a security incident and a compliance call. Fix: redact at the logging layer, not by hoping developers remember.
- **Logs with no retention plan.** You keep everything forever until the bill or the disk forces a panicked delete of exactly the window you needed. Fix: decide retention and sampling up front, tiered by level.

**Bottom line:** logs are written for the person debugging at 3am, not for the person writing the code at noon. The rule: if a line can't be searched, correlated, and acted on under pressure, it isn't a log — it's disk you rented to store noise.

items.title: [tech] A retry without a budget is a denial-of-service you wrote yourself
items.content_text:
# A retry without a budget is a denial-of-service you wrote yourself
STATUS: DRAFT

Two decades of shipping backend systems taught me that the outage that hurts most is rarely the one the vendor caused — it's the one your own retry loop amplified. I've watched a single flaky downstream turn into a full-region brownout because every caller retried instantly, three times, forever. The dependency blinked; our retry storm is what actually knocked it over.

Named failure modes I've paid for:
- **Retries with no cap.** Retrying "until it works" means retrying a dead service into the ground. Fix: bound every retry with a max attempt count AND a total time budget — whichever trips first, you stop.
- **No jitter.** Everyone retries on the same 1s/2s/4s schedule, so the herd hits the recovering service in perfect lockstep and re-kills it. Fix: exponential backoff with full jitter, always.
- **Retrying non-idempotent writes.** Retrying a POST that already succeeded but timed out on the response — now you've double-charged someone. Fix: idempotency keys, or don't retry writes at all.
- **Retrying at every layer.** Client retries 3x, gateway retries 3x, service retries 3x — that's 27 real calls per "one" request. Fix: retry at exactly one layer; everyone else fails fast.
- **No circuit breaker.** Hammering a service that's clearly down instead of shedding load and letting it breathe. Fix: trip a breaker after N failures, then probe gently before reopening.

**Bottom line:** a retry is a promise to do more work when things are already going badly. The rule: every retry needs a cap, jitter, an idempotency guarantee, and exactly one owner — otherwise you've written your own DoS and scheduled it for your worst day.

items.title: [tech] A healthcheck that can't fail is a green light to nowhere
items.content_text:
# A healthcheck that can't fail is a green light to nowhere
STATUS: DRAFT

Twenty years of on-call taught me the scariest dashboard is the all-green one, because green is only as honest as the check behind it. I've watched a `/health` endpoint return 200 while the app couldn't reach its database — the handler just returned `"ok"` as a string constant. Nobody wired the actual dependency into the probe.

Named failure modes I've been burned by:
- **The static 200.** The health route returns a hardcoded literal. It proves the web server is up, nothing else. Fix: the probe must touch the real dependency — do a `SELECT 1`, a queue ping, a cache read — and fail loudly when it can't.
- **The count-vs-count check.** You compare two copies of the same truncated source and call it validation. Both agree on the same wrong number. Fix: assert against ground truth (items on disk), not against a second cached copy.
- **The verifier that hangs.** A GET-based check that stalls headless looks like a failure of the thing you're checking, not the check. Fix: suspect the verifier's transport first — use HEAD, set a timeout, prove the instrument works.
- **The check nobody reads.** It runs, it fails, it logs to a file no alert watches. Fix: a failing check must page someone or block a deploy, or it's decoration.

The trap underneath all four: a check that can only pass is not a check, it's a comfort object.

**Bottom line:** green means nothing until you've watched the check go red on purpose. The rule: before you trust a healthcheck, break the dependency and confirm it fails — an unfalsifiable check is worse than none because it manufactures confidence you didn't earn.

items.title: [tech] A cache you can't invalidate is a second database you didn't mean to build
items.content_text:
# A cache you can't invalidate is a second database you didn't mean to build

STATUS: DRAFT

Twenty years in and the cache bugs still cost me the most sleep. Not because caching is hard — because the day you add one, you quietly forked your source of truth and told nobody, including yourself.

The named failure modes I've actually eaten:

1. **The TTL-as-a-prayer.** Someone sets a 300-second TTL "to be safe" and now every incident has a five-minute uncertainty window baked in. You push the fix, users still see the bug, and you burn an hour doubting your own deploy before realizing the cache is lying to you on a timer. A TTL is a guess about staleness tolerance — write down what that tolerance actually is or you're just decorating.

2. **The invalidation that fans out to nothing.** You invalidate the key you were thinking about and forget the three derived keys built on top of it. The list view refreshes, the detail view rots. Caught this one only because a user screenshotted two pages that disagreed with each other.

3. **The stampede.** Key expires, a thousand requests miss at once, all pile onto the origin, and the thing you added for speed becomes the thing that takes you down under load. A cache without a lock or a jittered refresh is a landmine that only arms itself when you're busy.

4. **The cache that outlived its schema.** You changed the shape of the object, deployed clean, and old serialized blobs deserialize into half-populated ghosts. Version your cache keys or a schema change becomes a haunting.

Fix: treat every cache as a database that needs an owner, a staleness budget written in plain words, key versioning on the object shape, and a stampede guard before it ever ships. If you can't answer "how do I know this is stale and how do I clear it," you haven't added a cache — you've added a bug with good latency.

**Bottom line:** caching moves your correctness problem somewhere darker and quieter. The rule: never add a cache until you can name exactly how it gets invalidated and who owns that.

items.title: [tech] A Timeout You Didn't Set Is a Timeout Someone Else Chose
items.content_text:
# A Timeout You Didn't Set Is a Timeout Someone Else Chose
STATUS: DRAFT

Twenty years wiring backend services together and the outages that scared me most weren't crashes — they were the hangs. A crash tells you where it died. A hang just sits there, holding a connection, while the queue behind it fills up and the whole system browns out in slow motion.

Named failure modes I've personally paid for:

**The default timeout of infinity.** Your HTTP client ships with no timeout, so the first time an upstream goes slow instead of down, every worker parks waiting on a socket that will never answer. I've watched a thread pool drain in under a minute because nobody set a read timeout and the dependency chose one for us: forever.

**The timeout longer than the caller's patience.** Your service waits eight seconds on a downstream, but the caller in front of you gave up at three and already retried. Now you're doing work for a request nobody's listening to anymore, three times over. Timeouts have to shrink as you go deeper, not grow.

**The retry stacked on top of a timeout with no budget.** Each layer retries three times, each waits five seconds, and four layers deep a single slow call becomes a two-minute pileup that looks exactly like an outage. The math multiplies and nobody did the multiplication.

What actually works: set an explicit timeout on every network call at the moment you write it, make each hop's deadline shorter than its caller's, and give the whole request one total budget that every retry draws down from — when the budget's gone, you fail fast instead of hanging hopeful.

**Bottom line:** a call without a timeout hasn't avoided the decision, it's delegated it to your slowest dependency on its worst day. The rule: if it crosses the network and you didn't set a deadline, you don't have a timeout — you have a hostage situation waiting to happen.

items.title: [tech] A Config Flag Is a Branch You Forgot to Test
items.content_text:
# A Config Flag Is a Branch You Forgot to Test
STATUS: DRAFT

Twenty years shipping backend systems and I've lost more nights to configuration than to code. The bug is never in the function you rewrote three times — it's in the YAML nobody reviews, the environment variable that means one thing in staging and the opposite in prod.

Named failure modes I've personally paid for:

**The flag that only exists in one environment.** Someone adds `ENABLE_NEW_PARSER=true` to prod by hand during an incident, it works, and it never makes it into the repo. Six months later a fresh deploy wipes it and the outage comes back with no code change to blame. Config that lives in a human's memory is config that will betray you.

**The default that's wrong when the key is missing.** Your code reads `timeout = config.get("timeout", 0)` and someone deletes the line. Now zero means "no timeout," every request hangs forever, and the connection pool drains in minutes. A missing config value should fail loud at boot, not silently pick the most dangerous default.

**Two sources of truth that drift.** The value is in the env var AND the config file, and one deploy reads one, the next reads the other. You spend an afternoon proving the code is identical across two boxes behaving differently, because the code IS identical — the config isn't. One value, one owner, one source.

**The untyped string that lies.** `DEBUG="false"` is a non-empty string, which is truthy, so debug mode runs in prod leaking stack traces to users. Config strings are not booleans until you parse them, and every `"false"` that ran as true has cost someone a security review.

What actually works: check config into version control, validate every key at startup and crash if it's malformed, keep exactly one source of truth per value, and diff config between environments in CI so a drift becomes a failed build, not a 2 a.m. page.

**Bottom line:** every config flag is an untested code branch you deployed anyway. The rule: if a value can change behavior in production and it isn't validated at boot and diffed in CI, you don't have configuration — you have a loaded gun with a config file for a safety.

items.title: [tech] A Retry Without a Budget Is a Self-Inflicted Outage
items.content_text:
# A Retry Without a Budget Is a Self-Inflicted Outage
STATUS: DRAFT

Twenty years building distributed systems and the single most common way I've watched teams turn a blip into an outage is the naive retry. A downstream service hiccups for 200ms, and the client library — helpfully — retries. Then every caller retries. Then their callers retry. You didn't recover from the incident; you manufactured a bigger one.

Named failure modes I've personally paid for:

**The retry storm with no jitter.** Every client backs off on the exact same doubling schedule, so they all wake up and hammer the recovering service in perfect synchronized waves. The service comes up, gets flattened in 50ms, goes down again. Without randomized jitter, backoff isn't backoff — it's a coordinated DDoS you wrote yourself.

**Retries on non-idempotent writes.** Someone slaps a retry wrapper on a POST that charges a card or creates an order. The first call actually succeeded; the response just got lost. Now you've double-charged the customer. If the operation isn't idempotent, a retry isn't resilience — it's a duplicate-side-effect generator.

**No retry budget across the stack.** Three layers each retry three times, and suddenly one user click becomes 27 downstream calls. The math compounds silently until a minor slowdown becomes a 27x load amplifier. You need a total retry budget for the whole request path, not per-layer optimism.

**Retrying errors that will never succeed.** A 400, a validation failure, an auth rejection — retried, on a loop, forever. You're burning capacity re-asking a question whose answer will never change. Retry transient failures only; fail fast on the permanent ones.

What actually works: exponential backoff WITH jitter, retry only idempotent operations (or make them idempotent with a request key), a shared retry budget per request, and a circuit breaker so you stop knocking on a door that's clearly not answering.

**Bottom line:** retries are borrowing capacity from a system that's already struggling. The rule: if you can't say what your total retry budget is for one user request, you don't have retries — you have an amplifier pointed at your own infrastructure.

items.title: [tech] A Dead-Letter Queue Nobody Reads Is a Landfill
items.content_text:
# A Dead-Letter Queue Nobody Reads Is a Landfill
STATUS: DRAFT

Twenty years shipping message-driven systems and I've watched the dead-letter queue become the place where accountability goes to die. Teams add a DLQ, feel safe, and never look at it again. It's not a safety net — it's a landfill with a nice name.

Named failure modes I've personally paid for:

**The DLQ with no alarm.** Messages fail, land in the DLQ, and sit there silently for six weeks because nobody wired a depth alert. The first person to notice is a customer asking why their order never shipped. A queue you don't alert on is a diary entry, not a recovery mechanism. Alarm on DLQ depth > 0, not > 1000.

**Redrive that replays the poison.** Someone finally drains the DLQ by blindly re-injecting everything into the main queue. The one malformed message that caused the failure just poisons the pipeline again, and now you've got a retry loop feeding its own graveyard. You need a triage step — inspect, fix or discard, THEN redrive — not a bulk replay button.

**No context on why it died.** The message is in the DLQ but the exception, the stack, the consumer version that choked on it — all gone. You're staring at a JSON blob with no idea what killed it. If you don't attach the failure reason as a message attribute at dead-letter time, you're doing forensics with the body but no cause of death.

**The DLQ that's actually a data-loss bucket.** Retention expires, messages age out, and the "we never lose data" claim quietly becomes false. A 14-day retention on a queue nobody checks weekly IS a delete button on a timer.

What actually works: alarm on depth immediately, attach the failure reason and consumer version at dead-letter time, triage before redrive, and put a human name against reviewing it on a schedule.

**Bottom line:** a DLQ is not where problems go to be safe — it's where they go to be seen. The rule: if no one owns reading the dead-letter queue on a cadence, you don't have error handling, you have deferred data loss.

items.title: [tech] A Cache Is a Second Source of Truth You Forgot to Govern
items.content_text:
# A Cache Is a Second Source of Truth You Forgot to Govern
STATUS: DRAFT

Twenty years in and I've watched more incidents born from caches than from the databases they were meant to protect. The moment you add a cache you've forked truth — and nobody put the fork on the org chart.

Named failure modes I've personally paid for:

**The thundering herd on expiry.** A hot key expires. Ten thousand requests miss simultaneously and all stampede the origin to recompute the same value. The database that was fine at cache-hit rates falls over in the first second of the miss. TTLs that all round to the same wall-clock minute turn every cache into a synchronized cliff. You need jittered TTLs and single-flight recomputation, not a prettier eviction policy.

**Stale writes that outlive the truth.** Someone updates the row, then a slow in-flight read races in and re-populates the cache with the OLD value it fetched before the write landed. Now the cache is confidently wrong and the database is right, and the bug report says "it fixes itself if I wait." That's the read-through race, and it's why write-invalidate-then-write ordering matters more than the cache library you picked.

**Caching the error.** An upstream returns a 500, and your cache-aside code cheerfully stores the empty/error response with the same TTL as a success. Now you're serving a cached failure to everyone for the full TTL. Negative results need their own short TTL and an explicit allowlist of what's cacheable.

**The invisible dependency.** A cache goes from optimization to load-bearing without anyone deciding it. Flush it for maintenance and the origin melts because it was never sized for real traffic. If your system can't survive a cold cache, the cache isn't a cache — it's an undocumented primary you can't fail over.

What actually works: jitter every TTL, single-flight the recompute, invalidate on write before you serve, cache negatives separately and briefly, and load-test with the cache emptied so you know the real floor.

**Bottom line:** a cache is a second source of truth wearing a performance costume. The rule: never add a cache without deciding its invalidation strategy, its cold-start survival, and who owns it — before it ships, not after the outage.

items.title: [tech] A healthcheck that only checks itself is theater
items.content_text:
# A healthcheck that only checks itself is theater
STATUS: DRAFT

Twenty years of on-call and the healthchecks that fooled me longest were the ones that returned 200 because the web server was up — while the database it needed was face-down in the mud. Green dashboard, dead product.

Named failure modes I've paid for:

- **The self-referential probe.** `/health` returns "OK" if the process can answer HTTP. It never touches the DB, the queue, or the downstream it can't live without. You're monitoring whether the light switch has power, not whether the room is lit.
- **The healthcheck that lies under load.** It passes in 5ms when idle, then the same endpoint takes 30s when the pool is exhausted — but your load balancer's timeout is 10s, so the node gets yanked exactly when it was recovering. You built a stampede.
- **The dependency you check but can't act on.** Probe says Redis is down, so the node marks itself unhealthy, so every node marks itself unhealthy, so you have zero capacity for a cache that was optional anyway. Correlated failure you wrote by hand.

The fix: a healthcheck must assert the thing the request actually needs (a real query, a real dependency ping with its OWN tight timeout), and it must degrade, not binary-flip. Distinguish "live" (restart me) from "ready" (route to me). k8s gives you both probes for a reason — most teams wire the same endpoint into both and wonder why rollouts thrash.

**Bottom line:** a probe that can't fail for the real reason is decoration. The rule: your healthcheck should be the first thing that goes red in an incident, not the last.

items.title: [tech] TECH — Observability is not monitoring (20-yr distributed-systems voice)
items.content_text:
# TECH — Observability is not monitoring (20-yr distributed-systems voice)
STATUS: DRAFT

**Hook:** After twenty years on call, I can tell you monitoring answers "is it down?" — observability answers "why is it weird?" — and most teams pay for the first while begging for the second.

**Body:**
The scar that taught me: a payments service passing every health check while a fraction of users silently got double-charged. Monitoring was green because the endpoint returned two-hundred. Nobody could ask "show me every request where the charge fired twice" because we logged counts, not events with correlation IDs. That's the whole difference — monitoring is pre-decided questions; observability is being able to ask a question you didn't anticipate.

Three failure modes I've watched sink teams. One: cardinality panic — they strip user and request IDs from metrics to save cost, then can't trace a single journey. Two: dashboard theater — twelve screens nobody reads, zero traces. Three: logs as a landfill — everything at INFO, so the one line that matters drowns.

The fix isn't a bigger vendor bill. It's structured events with a correlation ID threaded end to end, sampled smart, queryable after the fact.

**CTA:** Pick one incident from last month and ask: could you have answered it without deploying new logging? If no, you have monitoring, not observability.

**Bottom line:** Monitoring answers questions you set in advance; observability lets you ask new ones. The rule: if last month's incident needed fresh logging to explain, you don't have observability yet.

---
REVIEW GATE
- Brand-safe: Yes
- Non-generic: Yes (correlation-ID double-charge scar, three named failure modes)
- Real insight: Yes (monitoring = pre-set questions, observability = ad-hoc questions)
- Persona: 20-yr veteran — lived-experience framing, no fabricated stats
STATUS: APPROVED

items.title: [tech] A metric you don't alert on is a diary entry, not monitoring
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# A metric you don't alert on is a diary entry, not monitoring

Twenty years in and the postmortem line I've written most is some variant of "the
dashboard showed it the whole time." We had the graph. Nobody was looking at 3am.
A metric with no alert is a diary you read after the funeral.

Named failure modes I've paid for:
- **The vanity dashboard**: forty panels, all green, and the one that mattered was
  three scrolls down with no threshold on it. I've watched an on-call stare at a wall
  of graphs and still miss the SLO burn. Fix: every panel that can page you should page
  you; the rest belong in a report, not on the war-room screen.
- **Alerting on causes instead of symptoms**: paging on "CPU pegged" when the user impact
  is "checkout latency doubled." You get woken for noise and sleep through the outage.
  Fix: alert on the symptom your user feels, then use the cause metrics to debug.
- **The alert nobody trusts**: it fires so often on nothing that the team mutes it, and
  then it's decorative. I've seen a real incident ignored because "that thing always
  cries wolf." Fix: if an alert isn't actionable every time, it's a bug — fix or delete it.

The rule: monitoring is not the graph, it's the promise that someone gets woken when the
number that matters moves. If nothing pages, you don't have monitoring — you have history.

items.title: [tech] A feature flag you never remove is just tech debt with a toggle
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# A feature flag you never remove is just tech debt with a toggle

Twenty years in and the flag graveyard is real: I've inherited codebases where a third of
the flags were "temporary" rollouts from three years ago, each one a live `if` branch that
QA never covers and nobody dares delete. A flag is a promise to make a decision later. When
later never comes, you're paying interest on a loan you forgot you took.

Named failure modes I've paid for:
- **The permanent temporary**: a rollout flag defaulted on for everyone eighteen months ago,
  still wrapped in a conditional, still doubling the test matrix of every function it touches.
  Fix: every flag gets an expiry date and an owner at birth; a flag with no removal ticket
  doesn't merge.
- **The zombie branch**: the "off" path bit-rotted because nobody exercised it, then a
  panic rollback flipped the flag and shipped code that hadn't compiled cleanly in a year.
  Fix: if you keep the flag, you keep BOTH paths in CI — an untested off-path is a landmine,
  not a safety net.
- **The flag-on-flag combinatorial**: nested flags where the real behavior depended on four
  toggles nobody could reason about, so every incident started with "which combination is
  this box actually in?" Fix: flags are flat and independent, or they're a config object with
  one owner — never a decision tree you assemble at runtime.

The bottom line: a feature flag is a loan, not a feature. The rule: give every flag an owner
and an expiry the day you write it, and treat flag removal as part of shipping, not a chore
for a quarter that never arrives.

items.title: [tech] A retry without a cap is a DDoS you wrote against yourself
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# A retry without a cap is a DDoS you wrote against yourself

Twenty years in and the outage that still makes me wince wasn't caused by the failing
service — it was caused by everything downstream "helpfully" retrying it into the ground.
The dependency blipped for two seconds; the retries kept it down for twenty minutes.

Named failure modes I've paid for:
- **Synchronized retries**: every client retries on the same fixed interval, so the load
  arrives in perfect waves and the recovering service never gets a quiet window to stand
  up. I've watched a backend flap up-down-up because its own clients wouldn't let it
  breathe. Fix: full jitter on every backoff — randomize, never align.
- **Retries with no ceiling**: "keep trying until it works" quietly means "keep trying
  after the user has already left." I've seen a queue fill with retries for requests
  nobody was waiting on anymore. Fix: cap attempts AND bind them to the request deadline.
- **Retrying non-idempotent writes**: the first call actually succeeded, the response got
  lost, and the retry double-charged. Fix: idempotency keys on every write you'd retry.

The rule: a retry is a loaded weapon pointed at a service that's already hurt. Give it
jitter, a cap, and a deadline — or don't pull the trigger.

items.title: [tech] A cache you can't invalidate on demand is a bug with good latency
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# A cache you can't invalidate on demand is a bug with good latency

Twenty years in and the outages that scared me most weren't the loud ones — they were
the quiet stale reads. A cache makes the fast path fast and the wrong path invisible.
Nobody pages you for "correct but two hours old." The user just quietly gets a lie.

Named failure modes I've paid for:
- **The orphaned key**: we cached under one key shape, invalidated under another, and the
  two drifted the day someone renamed a field. Reads looked healthy; the data was fossil.
  Fix: derive the invalidation key from the exact same function that builds the read key —
  never hand-write it twice.
- **TTL as a prayer**: "it'll expire in five minutes" is not a correctness strategy, it's
  a bet that nobody notices for five minutes. I've watched a pricing bug ride a TTL
  straight into a customer invoice. Fix: for anything money- or trust-shaped, invalidate
  on write, and treat TTL as a safety net, not the plan.
- **Thundering herd on expiry**: everything expires at once, every request stampedes the
  origin, and the cache that was protecting the DB becomes the thing that kills it. Fix:
  jitter your TTLs and use a single-flight lock so one request refills while others wait.

The rule: if you can't name exactly what invalidates a cached value and prove it fires,
you don't have a cache — you have a scheduled outage with excellent p99.

items.title: [tech] A rollback plan you've never actually run is a wish, not a plan
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# A rollback plan you've never actually run is a wish, not a plan

Twenty years of deploys and the incident that still stings: we had a rollback
"procedure" in the runbook, everyone signed off on it, and the night we needed it
it took forty minutes to discover step 3 hadn't worked since a schema change six
months earlier. A rollback you haven't executed under load is a hypothesis.

Named failure modes I've paid for:
- **The one-way migration**: someone shipped a destructive schema change with no
  down-path, so "rolling back" the code left it pointed at a table that no longer
  matched. I've watched a team choose between two broken states at 2am. Fix:
  expand-and-contract — add columns, dual-write, backfill, and only drop the old
  shape a full deploy cycle later when rollback is still safe.
- **Rollback that skips the cache**: we reverted the binary but the poisoned
  entries lived on in a warm cache, so the "rolled back" system kept serving the
  bug. Fix: rollback plans name every stateful layer, not just the artifact.
- **Never rehearsed**: the plan was written once and never run, so nobody knew it
  had rotted. Fix: rehearse rollback in staging on a schedule, same as a fire drill.

The rule: if you can't cleanly roll back a change, you haven't finished designing
it. Rehearse the down-path or admit you're shipping without a net.

items.title: [tech] Backfills are outages in slow motion
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# Backfills are outages in slow motion

Twenty years in and the scariest deploy I've ever watched wasn't a feature — it was
a "quick backfill." Teams treat backfills as chores. They're not. A backfill is a
production write path that runs unthrottled, against cold data, with none of the
guardrails your live traffic earned over years. I've paid for that mistake in a
weekend I don't get back.

Named failure modes I've personally cleaned up at bad hours:
- **The unthrottled backfill**: someone runs a one-off script that hammers the
  primary with a million updates as fast as it can, and replica lag balloons until
  live reads start serving stale rows. I've watched a "harmless" catch-up job take
  down checkout because it starved the exact same DB customers were paying against.
  Fix: rate-limit the backfill to a fraction of steady-state write capacity and
  watch replica lag as your throttle signal, not row count.
- **Backfill without idempotency**: the script dies halfway, someone reruns it from
  the top, and now half the rows are double-applied. I've traced a corrupted balances
  table to exactly this. Fix: make every backfill resumable and idempotent — key off
  the row, upsert, and record a high-water mark so a rerun converges.
- **No dry-run, no blast radius estimate**: the query looked fine in staging where
  the table was tiny, then matched ten times more rows in prod than anyone guessed.
  Fix: always run a COUNT first, print the blast radius, and require a human to
  acknowledge the number before the write phase runs.

The rule: treat every backfill like a controlled outage you're choosing to have —
throttled, resumable, and with the blast radius measured before the first write.

items.title: [tech] Idempotency is a contract, not a retry checkbox
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# Idempotency is a contract, not a retry checkbox

Twenty years in and I still see teams treat idempotency as a thing you sprinkle on
a handler when the on-call gets paged. It isn't a feature you add — it's a contract
you either honor at every layer or silently violate at the one that matters.

Named failure modes I've personally cleaned up at bad hours:
- **The at-least-once lie**: a queue promises at-least-once delivery, and the team
  writes the consumer as if it were exactly-once. I've watched a payment worker
  double-charge because a broker redelivered on a rebalance and the handler had no
  dedupe key. Fix: derive a stable idempotency key from the message payload, not the
  delivery, and check it before you touch anything with a side effect.
- **Idempotent read, non-idempotent write**: the API returns the same GET twice so
  everyone assumes the whole path is safe, but the underlying POST appends a row each
  time. I've traced a duplicated-order storm to exactly this gap. Fix: make the write
  upsert against the client-supplied key, so a retry converges instead of accumulates.
- **Keys that expire before retries do**: you store the idempotency key with a short
  TTL, the client retries after a network partition heals hours later, and the key is
  gone — so the "safe" retry runs fresh. Fix: keep keys at least as long as your
  longest realistic retry window, and treat that window as a documented number.

The rule: if an operation can be delivered twice, assume it will be, and make the
second delivery a no-op by design — not by luck at the layer nobody was watching.

items.title: [tech] Your cache is a second source of truth, and nobody agreed to that
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# Your cache is a second source of truth, and nobody agreed to that

Twenty years of shipping and the nastiest data bugs I've chased almost never lived in the
database. They lived in the cache — the layer everyone treats as a performance detail and
nobody treats as state. The moment a cache can return an answer the database wouldn't, you
have two sources of truth and a race to decide which one lies today.

Named failure modes I've personally paid for:
- **Cache-aside with no write path**: reads populate the cache, writes update the DB, and
  nothing invalidates. I've watched a pricing page serve a stale number for hours because
  the "obvious" TTL was a day. Fix: every write that changes a cached entity must invalidate
  or update that key in the same transaction boundary, not "eventually".
- **The thundering-herd on expiry**: a hot key expires, a thousand requests miss at once,
  and they all stampede the DB you were protecting. I've seen a cache take down the exact
  database it existed to shield. Fix: request coalescing plus jittered TTLs so keys don't
  expire in lockstep.
- **Serializing the schema into the cache**: you ship a struct change, old cached blobs
  deserialize wrong, and prod throws on data that looks fine at rest. Fix: version your
  cache keys with the schema, so a deploy misses cleanly instead of poisoning reads.

The rule: if it can answer a query, it's a database — give it invalidation, versioning, and
a failure story, or it will invent its own and bill you at the worst possible hour.

items.title: [tech] Your logs are not a database — stop querying them like one
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# Your logs are not a database — stop querying them like one

Twenty years in and I keep meeting teams who deleted their metrics budget because
"we can just grep the logs." Then an incident hits and they're paying a fortune to
scan terabytes to answer a question a cheap counter would have answered instantly.

Named failure modes I've personally paid for:
- **The grep-driven incident**: at 3am, needing p99 latency for one endpoint, and
  the only path is a full-text scan across a week of logs. I've watched the query
  itself add load to a system already on fire. Fix: emit a real metric (a counter or
  histogram) for anything you'll ever need under pressure — logs are for the story,
  metrics are for the alarm.
- **The cardinality bomb**: someone logs the full user ID / request URL as a
  structured field and points a dashboard at it. I've seen an indexing cluster fall
  over because a "harmless" field had millions of unique values. Fix: keep
  high-cardinality identifiers out of anything you aggregate on.
- **The retention lie**: a team assumes logs are their audit trail, then discovers
  retention silently rotated the exact window the auditor asked for. I've had to
  explain that gap in a room I did not enjoy being in. Fix: if it's a record you must
  keep, write it to a store built to keep records — not to a rotating log buffer.

The rule: logs answer "what happened here," metrics answer "how bad is it now,"
and a database answers "what is true." Ask each the question it was built for.

items.title: [tech] Your database is not a queue — stop making it one
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# Your database is not a queue — stop making it one

Twenty years in and the same pattern keeps walking in the door: a `status` column,
a cron that `SELECT ... WHERE status='pending'`, and a team convinced they've built
a job system. They've built a slow-motion outage generator.

Named failure modes I've personally paid for:
- **The polling stampede**: ten workers all polling the same table every second,
  each grabbing the same rows because nobody used `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.
  I've watched duplicate charges go out because two workers "claimed" the same row.
  Fix: real row-level claim with SKIP LOCKED, or use an actual broker.
- **The dead-tuple swamp**: every job flips a row through pending→done, and now your
 hot table is mostly dead tuples, autovacuum is drowning, and index bloat is eating your
 cache. I've seen query latency triple with zero traffic change. Fix: move terminal
  jobs to an archive table, or don't store ephemeral work in your system of record.
- **The invisible backlog**: a queue tells you depth and age; a status column tells you
  nothing until a customer emails asking where their thing is. I've been that person
  writing the ad-hoc `COUNT(*) GROUP BY status` at 2am. Fix: emit depth and oldest-age
  metrics from day one, whatever substrate you pick.

The rule: if the work is transient, put it somewhere built to forget. Databases are
built to remember — that's exactly the wrong instinct for a queue.

items.title: [tech] An alert nobody owns is a pager pointed at the void
items.content_text:
# An alert nobody owns is a pager pointed at the void

STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)

I've watched a production database fill its disk over nine quiet hours while the alert for it fired perfectly — into a Slack channel everyone had muted in 2019. The monitoring worked. The humans didn't exist. Twenty years in and I still see teams confuse "we have alerting" with "someone will act."

Named failure modes I've eaten:

- **The muted channel graveyard.** Alerts route to a channel created by someone who left the company. Nobody unmutes it because unmuting it means owning it. The alert fires, the incident happens anyway, and the postmortem says "alerting gap" when the gap was ownership.
- **The threshold set once, in anger.** Someone got paged at 3am, raised the threshold to make it stop, and now the alert only fires after the outage is already on the status page. Thresholds tuned for sleep, not for signal.
- **The alert with no runbook.** It fires, the on-call opens it, and the description says "disk usage high." High where? Do what? The responder spends forty minutes rediscovering what the alert author knew and never wrote down.
- **The flapping alert everyone trained themselves to ignore.** It cried wolf eleven times a week for months. The twelfth time it was the real thing, and the on-call swiped it away on muscle memory. I've watched that swipe cost a full weekend.
- **The escalation path to a person, not a role.** "Page Ramesh" worked great until Ramesh changed teams. The alert still pages Ramesh. Ramesh has feelings about this.

The fix that actually worked: every alert must have three fields or it doesn't ship — an owning rotation (a role, never a name), a runbook link with the first three commands to run, and a review date. Anything that flaps twice in a week gets fixed or deleted in that week; an ignored alert is worse than no alert because it trains the ignoring.

**Bottom line:** monitoring detects, but only ownership responds. The rule: no alert ships without an owning rotation, a runbook, and a deletion path — a pager pointed at the void is just noise with a budget.

items.title: [tech] A backup you never restore is a rumor
items.content_text:
# A backup you never restore is a rumor

STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)

I've sat in the incident bridge where the backup job had been green for two straight years — and the restore produced an empty tarball. Nobody had ever actually restored it. The green checkmark was measuring "the cron ran," not "the data survives." Those are different religions.

Named failure modes I've eaten:

- **The green-job illusion.** The backup script exits zero because it backed up an empty directory. The path moved during a refactor; the job never noticed. Monitoring the job instead of the artifact is monitoring your own optimism.
- **The credential rot.** Restore needs a service account that was deprovisioned in a security sweep eight months ago. You discover this at 3am, mid-outage, when the person who owned the account has left the company.
- **The same-blast-radius backup.** Backups stored in the same account, same region, same credentials as production. The ransomware that ate prod ate the backups with the same key, in the same hour.
- **The restore that takes longer than the business survives.** The full restore is technically possible — in nineteen hours. Nobody ever timed it. Your RTO was a slide, not a measurement.
- **The schema drift.** The dump restores fine into the schema from when the backup strategy was written. The application has migrated forward eleven times since. Restored data, unusable database.

The fix that actually worked: schedule restores, not just backups. A monthly game-day where someone restores into a scratch environment, boots the app against it, and signs off. Time it. Store one copy outside the production credential domain. Alert on artifact size and content deltas, not exit codes.

**Bottom line:** untested backups are a story you tell auditors. The rule: a backup only exists after you've restored it — put the restore on the calendar or admit you don't have backups.

items.title: [tech] A retry without a budget is an outage amplifier
items.content_text:
# A retry without a budget is an outage amplifier

STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)

I've watched a five-minute database blip become a two-hour outage because every client retried at the same instant, forever, with love. The database recovered; the retry storm killed it again. Twice. We weren't down because of the failure — we were down because of our recovery code.

Named failure modes I've eaten:

- **The synchronized stampede.** Every caller retries on a fixed interval, so the moment the dependency limps back up it gets hit by the entire backlog at once, in phase, like a battering ram with a cron schedule.
- **The infinite retry.** No cap, no deadline. A request from a user who closed the tab an hour ago is still faithfully retrying, burning connections that live traffic needs right now.
- **The retry inside a retry.** The client retries, the gateway retries, the service mesh retries. Three layers of three attempts each is twenty-seven requests wearing one request's badge. Nobody designed that multiplier; it emerged.
- **The retry on the unretryable.** A 400 gets retried as enthusiastically as a 503. You cannot retry your way out of a malformed request — you can only retry your way into a rate limit.
- **The silent success.** The first attempt actually landed; the timeout was on the response, not the work. The retry lands too, and now you've charged the customer twice and get to write that email.

The fix that actually worked: exponential backoff with jitter so callers desynchronize, a hard retry budget per request AND per service, retry only on errors that are provably transient, and idempotency keys so a duplicate attempt is a no-op instead of a double-charge. Circuit-break when the budget burns down — fail fast and shed load so the dependency gets air to recover.

**Bottom line:** retries are load you generate against a system that just told you it's drowning. The rule: back off with jitter, cap the budget, retry only the transient, and make every attempt idempotent — or your recovery logic becomes the incident.

# A rollback you never rehearsed is a rumor

Twenty years of deploys and the worst nights were never the bad release — they were the
moment we reached for the rollback and discovered it was a story we'd been telling
ourselves. "We can always roll back" is the most expensive sentence in operations when
nobody has actually done it since the schema changed.

Named failure modes I've paid for:
- **The one-way migration**: the app rolls back in thirty seconds, the database doesn't
  roll back at all. I've stood in a war room watching a "five minute revert" turn into a
  four-hour restore because a column was dropped on the way up. Fix: expand-then-contract,
  always — never ship a deploy whose predecessor can't read the data it leaves behind.
- **The config drift trap**: the old binary comes back but the feature flags, env vars,
  and secrets moved on without it. The rollback boots and immediately crashes on a config
  key that didn't exist last month. Fix: version config with the release, not beside it.
- **The untested restore**: backups that were green for two years and unreadable the one
  night it mattered. A backup is a hope; a restore is a fact. Fix: rehearse the restore on
  a schedule, in prod-shaped infra, with a timer running — and let the team feel how long
  it actually takes before an incident makes them learn it live.

The rule: a rollback is a feature. It gets designed, tested, and rehearsed like one, or
it doesn't exist — no matter what the runbook says.

items.content_text:
# A backup you never restored is a rumor

STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)

I've watched a company discover, at 2 a.m. with the primary database gone, that eighteen months of nightly backups were empty tarballs. The cron job ran. The green checkmark showed. Nobody had ever restored one. The backup system wasn't broken that night — it had been broken for a year and a half, and the only test anyone ever ran was the one that mattered.

Named failure modes I've eaten:

- **The green cron lie.** The job exits 0 because the dump command ran, not because it produced anything usable. A permissions change six months ago made it dump zero tables, and exit-code monitoring called that success every night since.
- **The backup of the wrong thing.** The snapshot covers the data volume but not the config, the encryption keys, or the schema migrations table. You restore the bytes and the application still can't boot, because the backup captured the body and left the skeleton.
- **The restore that takes longer than the business survives.** The backup is real, tested, complete — and takes 26 hours to restore over a link nobody benchmarked. Your RPO is fine; your RTO is a resignation letter.
- **The credentials buried in the rubble.** The restore runbook lives in the wiki. The wiki lives on the infrastructure that just died. I've watched teams locked out of their own recovery because the keys to the lifeboat were stored on the ship.
- **The same-region snapshot.** Backups sitting in the same account, same region, same blast radius as production. One compromised admin key or one regional outage takes both. That's not a backup, that's a copy standing next to the original.

The fix that actually worked: schedule restores, not just backups. Once a month, restore to a scratch environment, boot the app against it, run a smoke query, and record how long the whole thing took. Print the runbook. Keep restore credentials somewhere that survives the disaster you're planning for.

**Bottom line:** nobody needs backups — everybody needs restores, and only one of those is ever tested by accident. The rule: a backup doesn't exist until you've restored it, timed it, and booted the app on top of it.

items.content_text:
# A timeout you copied is a decision you never made

STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)

I've watched a whole payment stack fall over because every service in the call chain shipped with the same default 30-second timeout — copied from a blog post, from a template, from the service next door. When the database slowed down, nothing failed fast. Everything failed together, thirty seconds late, holding every thread hostage on the way down.

Named failure modes I've eaten:

- **The default nobody chose.** The client library ships with 30s, the framework with 60s, and your code with whatever the last person pasted. Ask the team what the timeout *should* be for that call and you get silence — nobody ever decided, so the incident decided for them.
- **The inverted pyramid.** The edge times out at 10s but the service it calls waits 30s on its downstream. The edge gives up, retries, and now the backend is doing the same expensive work twice for a caller that already hung up.
- **The retry multiplying the timeout.** Three retries times a 30-second timeout is a 90-second worst case that nobody budgeted, sitting behind a load balancer with a 60-second cap. The user sees a 502 while your service is still faithfully working.
- **The timeout with no deadline.** Each hop has a local timeout but nothing carries a total budget. Hop four spends time hop one already promised away. The request is dead at the edge and alive in the core, and your metrics call that success.
- **The connection timeout masquerading as a read timeout.** Someone set "the timeout" to 5s — connect only. The socket connects instantly and then reads forever. The knob you tuned wasn't the knob that hurt you.

The fix that actually worked: make timeouts a designed number, not an inherited one. Start from the caller's budget at the edge, subtract per hop, and propagate the remaining deadline down the chain. Set read and connect separately. Cap total retry time, not retry count. And put every timeout in config next to a comment saying who chose it and why — because the next incident will ask.

**Bottom line:** every timeout in your system is a decision — the only question is whether a person made it or an outage did. The rule: budget at the edge, propagate the deadline, and never ship a timeout you can't explain.

Guard that account like the outage depends on it — because it does.

# A backup you never restore is a hope, not a plan

STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)

I've watched a team discover, at two in the morning during a real incident, that eighteen months of nightly backups were empty tarballs. The cron job was green. The dashboard was green. The files were zero bytes. Nobody had ever run a restore. In twenty years of shipping infrastructure I have never once seen a backup fail loudly — they fail silently and get discovered at the worst possible moment.

Named failure modes I've paid for:

- **The green-lie cron.** The backup script exits zero because the *script* ran, not because the *dump* succeeded. The database connection failed, the error went to a log nobody reads, and the exit code lied for a year.
- **The credential rot.** The backup service account's password got rotated during a security sweep. Backups stopped. Alerting was wired to job failure, not to data freshness, so nothing fired.
- **The same-blast-radius copy.** Backups written to the same disk array, same account, same region as production. The ransomware — or the fat-fingered delete — took both in one motion.
- **The restore nobody has run.** The backup is fine; the restore procedure is a wiki page written by someone who left. Missing schema step, wrong version of the tool, four hours of guessing while the business bleeds.
- **The retention illusion.** Thirty days of dailies sounds fine until the corruption happened forty days ago and every "good" backup you have is a faithful copy of bad data.

The fix that actually worked for us: schedule the *restore*, not the backup. Once a month, restore to a scratch environment, run a checksum and a row-count sanity check against production, and time the whole thing. Alert on data freshness — "newest restorable copy is older than N hours" — never on job exit codes. Keep at least one copy in a different account and different failure domain, with credentials that production cannot touch.

**Bottom line:** nobody wants backups; everybody wants restores. The rule: a backup is not real until you've restored from it, timed it, and verified the bytes — everything before that is a hope with a schedule.

items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# A retry without a budget is a self-inflicted DDoS

Twenty years of on-call and the outages that scared me most weren't caused by attackers — they
were caused by our own clients being loyal. A dependency hiccuped for thirty seconds, and every
caller retried instantly, forever, in sync. The hiccup healed; the retry storm did not.

Named failure modes I've paid for:
- **The immediate retry loop**: fail, retry, fail, retry, no delay, no cap. I've watched a
  service survive its outage and then die from the recovery, because ten thousand clients hit
  it the same second it came back. Fix: exponential backoff with jitter, always — the jitter is
  not optional, it's the part that breaks the synchronized stampede.
- **Retrying the non-retryable**: hammering a four-hundred-class error like it's a network blip.
  A bad request is bad the tenth time too. Fix: classify before you retry; only transient
  failures earn another attempt.
- **No retry budget**: every layer retries three times, five layers deep, and one user click
  becomes hundreds of backend calls. I've traced a single page load fanning out into a small
  flood. Fix: budget retries at ONE layer, propagate a deadline, and let the rest fail fast.

The rule: a retry is a loan against the downstream system's recovery. Take it with a budget, a
backoff, and jitter — or you're not being resilient, you're being the incident.

shrug. If you can't diff it, you can't own it, and nobody owns what they can't see change.

Named failure modes I've paid for:
- **The console-clicked change**: someone edits a value in a web UI, no PR, no history, and

The rule: infrastructure you can't diff is infrastructure you can't reason about. If a change
can't produce a two-column before/after with a name attached, it's not a change you control —
it's a liability with a timestamp.

items.title: [tech] A cache you can't invalidate is a bug with a countdown
items.content_text:
# A cache you can't invalidate is a bug with a countdown

STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)

I've shipped a cache that made the demo fly and then spent the next quarter explaining to support why a fraction of users saw stale prices for hours. Caching isn't free speed — it's a promise that the world hasn't changed, and that promise expires when you're not looking.

Named failure modes I've watched trap people (myself first):

- **The TTL nobody chose.** Someone typed a round number of seconds because it felt safe, with zero connection to how often the underlying data actually changes. Now you're either serving stale data or hammering the origin — and nobody can tell you which.
- **The unbounded key space.** You cache per-user, per-query, per-permutation, and the key set grows without limit. The cache becomes a memory leak with good PR, and the eviction storm hits at peak traffic.
- **The invalidation that lies.** You clear the key on write, but a read-replica lag or a second cache layer still holds the old value. You "invalidated" it and the stale value is right there, mocking your log line.
- **The thundering herd.** The hot key expires, a thousand requests miss simultaneously, and they all stampede the origin at once. The cache designed to protect the database becomes the reason it falls over.
- **The cache as source of truth.** It started as an optimization and quietly became the only place some data lives. The day it flushes, you learn what you actually lost.

The fix that held: tie every TTL to a real change frequency you can name, bound the key space with explicit eviction, and make invalidation a tested path — not a hopeful `delete`. For hot keys, use a lock or stale-while-revalidate so one miss refreshes while the rest serve the last-good value.

**Bottom line:** a cache is a bet that the past is still true. The rule: name the TTL from real change rates, bound and test eviction, and never let a cache quietly become the only copy of anything.

items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# A timeout without a total budget is just a slower way to fail

Twenty years of production and the incident I keep reliving: every service in the chain
had a "sane" timeout, and the whole request still hung for the better part of a minute
because nobody added them up. Local timeouts feel responsible. Chained, they compound
into a number no user will ever wait for.

Named failure modes I've paid for:
- **The additive stall**: service A waits on B waits on C, each with a generous timeout,
  and the caller inherits the sum. I've watched a page "load" long after the human left.
  Fix: set a request-level deadline at the edge and pass it down; each hop gets what's
  left, not a fresh clock.
- **Retry amplification**: a timeout triggers a retry which triggers a retry, and now one
  slow dependency becomes a self-inflicted traffic storm. I've seen a healthy backend
  knocked over by its own clients retrying. Fix: retries share the deadline; when the
  budget's gone, you fail fast, not louder.
- **The infinite fallback**: the "graceful" fallback path had no timeout at all because
  nobody thought it'd get hit. It got hit. Fix: every path that touches the network,
  including the sad path, carries the deadline.

The rule: timeouts are local; budgets are global. Ship a deadline that travels with the
request, and let every hop spend from the same shrinking wallet.
