items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (manual gate, veteran-voice)
# The pause is the punchline — 20 years of dying and learning why

New comics fear silence, so they talk through it. That's the single most expensive habit
on stage. The laugh lives in the gap after the setup — step on it and you've refunded the
audience their tension for free.

Scar tissue, catalogued:
- **The nervous tag**: you deliver the punchline, panic in the silence, and add a weaker
  second punchline on top. Now the audience doesn't know which one to laugh at, so they
  laugh at neither. I did this for two straight years.
- **Racing the drink order**: in bar rooms, timing a punchline while the blender runs is
  amateur hour. Watch the bar, not just the crowd — hold the line until the noise floor drops.
- **Uniform pacing**: if every bit has the same rhythm, the crowd predicts your punchlines
  and beats you to them. Vary setup length like a pitcher varies speed.

The drill that fixed me: record a set, count the beats you left after each punchline.
If it's under two, you're stealing from your own laughs. Silence isn't the absence of
material — it's the material working.

items.title: [comedy] Crowd Work Is a Crutch (Said the Guy With a Broken Leg)
items.content_text:
# Crowd Work Is a Crutch (Said the Guy With a Broken Leg)
STATUS: DRAFT — NOT POSTED | persona: 20-yr club comic | 2026-07-24

Every scene has that comic who "kills" every night and hasn't written a new minute since 2019. All crowd work. Ask them to do six clean minutes for a TV taping and you can hear their soul leave the building.

Here's what two decades of open mics taught me: crowd work is a skill AND an avoidance behavior, and the difference is what you do Tuesday afternoon. If you're riffing because the room demands it — great, that's the job. If you're riffing because facing your notebook feels like a dental appointment — that's not stage presence, that's procrastination with a microphone.

The named failure mode: "the front-row dependency." You build a set that needs a talkative accountant in seat 3 to function. Then you get booked on a corporate gig where everyone's boss is watching and nobody will say their own name out loud. Your act now has a missing dependency, and there's no npm install for charisma.

The fix that works: one written minute for every ten minutes of crowd work you perform. Non-negotiable ratio. The written stuff is your pension; crowd work is your tips.

CTA: What's the deadest room you've ever had to work without a single volunteer?

items.title: [comedy] Premise hoarding: the notebook full of jokes you'll never tell
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — NOT SENT

# Premise hoarding: the notebook full of jokes you'll never tell

Twenty years of open mics and green rooms, and the failure mode that quietly kills more comics than bombing ever does is **premise hoarding** — a notebook stuffed with "funny ideas" that never touch a stage because the comic is waiting until the bit is "ready." The bit is never ready. Stage time is the editor, not the notebook.

I hoarded for my first three years. I had forty pages of premises and about four working minutes. Meanwhile the guy who started the same month as me had fifteen minutes that killed, built from maybe ten premises he'd dragged on stage half-baked and rewritten in front of audiences. The audience wrote his act. My notebook wrote mine, and my notebook wasn't funny.

What I learned the slow, humiliating way:

- **A premise gets three mic attempts, then a verdict.** Laughs somewhere? Keep digging. Silence three times in different rooms? Cut it or shelve it. Rooms differ, but three cold rooms is data, not bad luck.
- **Write the tag on stage, not at the desk.** My best tags all came from riffing when a bit was dying and I had nothing to lose. Desperation is a better writer than comfort.
- **Record every set.** Not to admire yourself — to catch the accidental phrasings that got the laugh you didn't plan. Half my act is transcribed accidents.
- **New material nights exist for a reason.** Burning a paying-crowd set on untested stuff is arrogance; never testing is cowardice. Use the room built for the mess.

The rule: a premise in the notebook is worth nothing until it has failed on stage at least once. Get it up, let it die, rebuild it from what the room told you.

items.title: [comedy] A callback is earned, not planted
items.content_text:
STATUS: DRAFT — reviewed (content_gate, veteran-voice)
# A callback is earned, not planted

Twenty years of rooms and the callback is still the most misused move in comedy. New
comics decide in the notebook that line four will "come back" at the end, then force it
whether the room bought the original or not. A callback only lands if the first laugh was
real. You're not planting a seed — you're cashing a check the room already wrote.

Scar tissue, catalogued:
- **The forced return**: bringing back a premise that got a polite chuckle, not a laugh,
  so the callback plays to silence and now two bits are dead. I did this for years. Fix:
  only call back what actually crushed; if the setup underperformed, cut the payoff live.
- **Over-milking**: the callback hits, so you go back a third and fourth time until the
  room feels worked instead of surprised. Fix: one great return beats three diminishing
  ones — leave on the biggest one.
- **Callback with no time gap**: referencing a bit thirty seconds later isn't a callback,
  it's a repeat. The magic is the distance; the room has to almost forget.

The rule: don't script the callback, script the setup and let the room tell you if it
earned one. The best callbacks are decisions you make on stage, not in the notebook.

items.title: [comedy] Bit: "Have you tried turning your whole life off and on again"
items.content_text:
# Bit: "Have you tried turning your whole life off and on again"

**Vertical:** comedy | **Format:** stand-up bit / Reel script | **Date:** 2026-07-23

---

Twenty years writing jokes and the ones that land aren't clever — they're *recognized*. Here's a tight 45-second bit built on a universal, escalated three times. Delivery notes in brackets.

---

You ever notice tech support only knows one spell? [beat] "Have you tried turning it off and on again." That's it. That's the whole religion.

And the worst part — it *works*. Which is insulting. I spent forty minutes describing the problem like I'm at a crime scene, and the fix is the emotional equivalent of "have you tried not thinking about it." [pause]

I've started using it on everything. Car won't start? Turn it off and on again. [mimes key] Relationship falling apart? [flat] "Babe, have you tried leaving and coming back? Just — cold boot the marriage."

[build] My doctor said my cholesterol's high. I said, "Have you tried turning me off and on again?" He said that's called death. I said, "So it IS an option." [land]

---

Why it works: the callback structure. Same phrase, three contexts, each higher stakes — mundane (car), emotional (relationship), existential (death). The last line reframes the running joke as literally fatal, which is the surprise. Don't over-explain the medical one; the flat delivery does the lifting. Kill any adjective you're tempted to add — specificity is funny, decoration is not.
